Understanding your users shouldn't feel like guesswork, but without the right tools, it often does. If you've ever stared at analytics wondering why users drop off, rage-click, or abandon a form halfway through, you're not alone.
That's where session replay software comes in.
Industry outlook backs this up: the session replay software market is projected to grow to $744.27 million by 2031, growing at a CAGR of 13.83% , reflecting rapid adoption across product, UX, and engineering teams.
These tools let you watch real user sessions: every scroll, click, and hesitation, so you can pinpoint friction, uncover hidden bugs, and improve your site's UX with confidence.
How did I find and evaluate these top session replay software?
I spent weeks testing session replay software, narrowing down the best options based on features, ease of use, pricing, and real user feedback. I also used AI-driven research to analyze software updates, marketer preferences, and common challenges to ensure these recommendations are as accurate and helpful as possible.
I also looked into which session replay software is most reliable for app developers, with special attention to tools that offer debugging logs, crash insights, and mobile SDK support.
In cases where I couldn't personally test a tool due to limited access, I consulted a professional with hands-on experience and validated their insights using verified G2 reviews. The screenshots featured in this article may be a mix of those captured during testing and those obtained from the vendor's G2 page.
My research and analysis are also based on real-time buyer sentiments and the proprietary G2 scores each session replay software offers. I reviewed expert opinions on the best session replay software, pulling verified insights from developers, product managers, and UX analysts featured on G2.
What makes the best session replay software worth it: My perspective
As I evaluated different session replay tools, I realized that watching user behavior in real time is powerful. Some platforms gave me crystal-clear insights, while others left me with more questions than answers.
I realized that the best session replay software isn't just about recording sessions. It's about helping you understand them. Here are the features I paid close attention to while testing these tools:
High-quality, smooth replays: I look for smooth, high-resolution recordings that clearly show mouse movement, clicks, scrolls, and interactions with forms or dynamic elements. If I have to guess what happened, the replay's not doing its job.
Advanced filtering and segmentation: Filters are a lifesaver when you have hundreds of sessions to sift through. I rely on them to surface sessions that actually matter: rage clicks, exit pages, device types, traffic source, country, you name it.
Error tracking and console logs: Some tools log JavaScript errors and failed API calls directly within the session playback. I found this super useful when trying to understand where things went wrong on a page, without needing to dig through dev tools separately.
Event tracking and heatmaps: I like it when tools also provide click maps, scroll maps, and attention heatmaps . These give me a macro view of what users are doing across a page, so I can combine that with the micro-level insights from replays for a more complete picture.
AI-powered session summaries and anomaly detection: The best tools now surface patterns automatically, flagging struggle points, summarizing sessions in natural language, and alerting teams to friction before anyone has to hunt for it. This is where 2026 tools have moved well beyond basic recording.
User journey mapping and funnels: Tools that visualize funnels alongside replays make it easier to spot patterns and optimize the entire user flow, not just individual pages. These features made certain platforms stand out as recommended session recording apps for improving my user interface.
Lightweight script and performance impact: If a tool slows down your site, that's a dealbreaker. The best ones run in the background without affecting the user experience or page speed.
Over the span of several weeks, I compared close to 25+ session replay software. I narrowed down the best seven based on their features and ease of use.

When it comes to debugging and understanding how users interact with an app, LogRocket is one of the tools users lean on the most. Rated 4.6/5 on G2 with over 2,300 reviews, LogRocket pairs session replays with a built-in console and network capture to help teams diagnose issues faster.
What really stands out is how much detail it captures.
From network requests and console logs to Redux state and JavaScript errors , everything is neatly tied to the exact moment it happened in the session.
That context makes finding and fixing issues way faster.
Teams love how session replays line up with console logs, network calls, and state changes, so engineers, PMs, and designers can move from "what happened?" to "fixed" much faster.
What also makes LogRocket sticky for engineering teams is how it connects to the tools they already use.
Jira, GitHub, Datadog, and Intercom are all supported, so issues identified in session replay get routed directly into the dev workflow without any context-switching.
Several G2 reviewers call this out specifically as the reason LogRocket becomes the default tool across their entire support and engineering cycle, not just a debugging aid used occasionally.
Another capability worth noting is Galileo AI , LogRocket's AI that continuously watches session replays, reads support tickets, and surfaces user struggles automatically.
It routes fixes directly into developer workflows, including integrations with AI coding tools, so instead of digging for problems, teams get alerted to what matters most and handed the context they need to act.
Session search and filtering can feel cumbersome at high volume.
Searches often default to user email rather than more flexible identifiers, and building the right query or graph takes some learning, particularly for first-time users.
Once teams get comfortable with the filter logic, it clicks, but the combination of Galileo AI and dedicated onboarding support means most teams get there faster than expected.
Overall, G2 review data consistently frames LogRocket as a dependable, insight-rich tool. If you budget appropriately and give your team a quick orientation on filters and views, you get a powerful, reliable way to spot friction, prioritize fixes, and keep the user experience moving in the right direction.
What I like about LogRocket:
The fact that I can view console logs, network activity, Redux state, and even JavaScript errors within each session is a huge plus. It cuts down on back-and-forth and helps me pinpoint bugs way faster.
I really like how Galileo AI watches sessions proactively and surfaces issues before they become patterns. It's like having a smart assistant monitoring everything in the background.
What G2 users like about LogRocket:
"As a manager of a technical support team in the SaaS space, I've found LogRocket incredibly useful.
The ability to quickly locate user sessions through its convenient UI and see exactly what a user did while using our product has been a huge help.
The tools for navigating sessions are extensive and snappy, and integrating LogRocket with our application was very straightforward."
- LogRocket review , Michael W.
What I dislike about LogRocket:
Session search defaults to user email rather than more flexible options, and building custom queries takes effort, but once the filter logic is familiar, it becomes a genuine time-saver for surfacing the sessions that matter most.
Replay performance can slow down on longer sessions, which adds friction when diagnosing issues in extended user flows, though a quick page refresh typically resolves it and doesn't affect the underlying data.
What G2 users dislike about LogRocket:
"The UI for metrics is slow and clunky, it often takes an incredibly long time for simple metrics to load, and creating and refining custom graphs is not super intuitive."
- LogRocket review , Verified User

When I first got my hands on PostHog , I wasn't expecting it to be this loaded. It felt like someone took everything I needed for product analytics, session replay, and feature flagging, and wrapped it into one tool and then somehow made it free to start with.
The all-in-one approach is genuinely hard to beat.
Session replays, feature flags, funnels, product analytics, and experimentation all live in the same platform, connected to the same customer data model.
Product and engineering teams can ship, measure, and iterate without stitching five separate tools together, and that reduction in tool sprawl alone changes how fast teams move.
The open source foundation and free tier are real differentiators.
The first 5,000 session recordings are free every month, usage-based pricing scales transparently, and teams that want full control can self-host.
Compared to tools that lock core features behind expensive plans, PostHog's pricing model is refreshingly predictable, something several G2 reviewers specifically call out as a reason they stayed.
The developer experience is another strength.
PostHog integrates quickly across Next.js, React Native, SvelteKit, and Kotlin Multiplatform, and custom event tracking gives teams precise control over what gets measured.
For founders or product teams, PostHog is arguably the best session replay tool for SaaS startups, offering developer-focused features without enterprise pricing.
Setting up events, funnels, and dashboards properly takes planning, and non-technical teammates often need some guidance before the advanced analysis features feel natural.
The platform is genuinely powerful once configured well, but teams new to product analytics should expect a ramp-up period.
The good news is that PostHog's self-serve documentation and responsive support team mean most teams get productive faster than the initial learning curve suggests.
Notable patterns in G2 reviews position PostHog as a high-value pick for SaaS teams that want developer-friendly analytics with session replay built in. A short onboarding, saved views, and a few internal how-tos usually unlock the upside: faster debugging, tighter product loops, and fewer tool handoffs.
What I like about PostHog:
PostHog brings everything together: session replays, feature flags, event tracking, user profiles, and dashboards. I don't need to juggle multiple tools anymore.
The fact that it's open source with a free tier that's actually useful made it a no-brainer for me. Plus, the pricing model is super clear, no sneaky costs popping up later.
What G2 users like about PostHog:
"PostHog is one of the most useful tools for understanding what users actually do inside a product.
I really like that analytics, funnels, session recordings, feature flags, experiments, surveys, and dashboards are all connected in one place, rather than being split across several different tools.
The session replay feature is especially valuable because it lets us observe real user behavior, spot friction points, and better understand where and why users drop off."
- PostHog review , Amirhossein A.
What I dislike about PostHog:
Setting up events, funnels, and dashboards properly takes planning, particularly for teams without a strong analytics background, but once the tracking structure is in place, the depth of insight it unlocks is hard to match at this price point.
Documentation covers the basics well, but thins out for advanced edge cases, and the in-app AI bot hits the same ceiling since it draws from the same source material, though PostHog's community and support team tend to fill that gap reliably.
What G2 users dislike about PostHog:
"Parts of the UI and navigation can start to feel overwhelming as you adopt more PostHog features over time.
There's a lot of power packed into the platform, but it can sometimes take too many clicks or a bit of context switching to get to exactly what you're looking for.
Query performance on larger datasets can also occasionally feel slow or inconsistent."
- PostHog review , Natanael G.
Session replay tells you what users did. Product analytics software tells you why they did it at scale; together, they give you the full picture.
Microsoft Clarity is an epic tool that is completely free. Like, no hidden upgrade tiers, no "limited access", just everything unlocked from the jump. Clarity is one of the leading session replay solutions for small businesses, offering unlimited features for free with zero technical setup barriers.
Setup is straightforward: installed via Google Tag Manager, Clarity is typically up and running in minutes, no developer lift or lengthy implementation guides required, which isn't the case with many analytics tools.
The native GA4 integration is a major plus; teams can pair Clarity's session-level insights with broader traffic and conversion data from Google Analytics to see not just who visited, but why they bounced or converted.
The core feature set delivers immediate value.
Heatmaps show which page elements attract attention and which get ignored.
Scroll maps reveal how far visitors actually read, which is useful for content placement and above-the-fold decisions.
Session recordings layer in the qualitative "why": watching real users navigate a flow surfaces design snags, broken elements, and confusing patterns that raw numbers alone would never expose.
Worth noting is the recent addition of Copilot AI in Clarity , which generates natural language session takeaways and can answer questions about your data directly, all still at no cost. For lean teams that want AI-assisted insight without paying for a premium tier, this is a meaningful upgrade to an already strong free offering.
Clarity doesn't support custom event tracking or funnel creation, which means teams that need to fire events, filter recordings by those events, or build conversion funnels will hit a ceiling fairly quickly.
It's a real limitation for anyone moving beyond behavioral observation into experimentation or conversion optimization.
Pairing Clarity with GA4 goals and journeys covers a good portion of this gap while the tool remains free.
G2 review data continues to position Clarity as a high-value option for lean teams: no-cost capture, straightforward heatmaps, and dependable session replays. If you pair Clarity with GA4 goals and journeys, set simple filter presets, and export key clips periodically, you retain most of its benefits while sidestepping the common limitations.
What I like about Microsoft Clarity:
It's totally free and packed with features. I still can't believe Clarity gives me unlimited session recordings and heatmaps without charging a dime. For a free tool, it feels surprisingly full-featured.
The Copilot AI integration is a genuine bonus: getting natural language session summaries and data answers without needing a paid plan feels like a real step forward for lean teams.
What G2 users like about Microsoft Clarity:
"I really value using Microsoft Clarity for watching session recordings.
It's great that it saves all recordings for a long time, unlike other tools where I can't keep recordings for more than 30 days.
This long-term storage is super efficient for finding where users struggle and detecting UX issues.
It allows me to analyze a user's entire journey, for instance, when a user churns, which helps me find qualitative product patterns."
- Microsoft Clarity review , Samir M.
What I dislike about Microsoft Clarity:
Clarity doesn't support custom event tracking or funnel creation, which means teams that need to fire events and filter recordings by them will hit that ceiling sooner than expected, though the GA4 integration helps bridge the gap for basic conversion tracking at no extra cost.
Replay updates aren't truly real-time, so reviewing a just-completed session sometimes means waiting, which slows live debugging, though this is a minor trade-off for a tool that costs nothing and installs in minutes.
What G2 users dislike about Microsoft Clarity:
"I wish it could compare (measure and report) on previous periods, and also provide AI insights when comparing user behavior across different campaigns."
- Microsoft Clarity review , David C.
Turn insights from session replays into real experiments with A/B testing tools to start optimizing your UX with data-driven decisions.
Fullstory can shift teams from guessing about user issues to observing them in real time. Rated 4.5/5 on G2 with over 1,000 reviews, session replays capture scrolls, clicks, rage-clicks, hovers, and more, providing a clear picture of how users actually experience a site: not just what they clicked, but how they interacted.
What sets Fullstory apart from most tools in this category is its autocapture approach.
Every interaction is recorded automatically, no manual event tagging, no instrumentation plan required before you start.
That means teams can go back and answer questions about user behavior retroactively, even for events they didn't think to track at the time.
For product teams that are constantly evolving what they want to measure, that flexibility is a significant advantage over tools that require upfront event setup before any data exists.
Fullstory's heatmaps, scroll maps, and funnels help pinpoint drop-offs and stuck points, making it easier to validate A/B tests and refine user flows . Teams often make targeted adjustments, like headline or CTA changes, based on these visual insights and see measurable conversion lifts.
Support is where Fullstory consistently stands apart.
G2 reviewers frequently highlight the customer success team by name, calling out their responsiveness, their willingness to help configure custom events and dashboards, and their proactive approach to shortening time to value.
For teams that invest in the enablement side, Fullstory rewards that investment quickly.
For very large sites or high-traffic environments, the sheer volume of captured behavioral data can make it harder to focus on what needs fixing first.
Building complex segments and metrics takes time, and working through large datasets requires some enablement before the platform fully opens up.
Once that structure is in place, though, the depth of behavioral insight Fullstory provides makes the investment pay off clearly.
G2 reviews describe Fullstory as a high-impact choice for understanding digital behavior at scale. If you budget for volume, set clear export and BI workflows, and give power users a bit of enablement, you get a platform that consistently reveals friction, informs A/B ideas, and shortens the path from signal to shipped improvements.
What I like about Fullstory:
The customer support team? Amazing. Every time I've hit a wall, they've been there to help. They're quick, they actually listen, and they take feedback and turn it into product improvements.
I love that Fullstory captures everything automatically without me having to set up events in advance. I've been able to go back and answer questions about user behavior I didn't even think to track when we first deployed it.
What G2 users like about Fullstory:
"The tool is robust and useful to help me determine the performance of our site as well as help me identify issues before the customer expresses them.
The ability to match a customer concern with a session has helped us better understand issues from the video recordings.
The MCP/Claude integration also helps me explain what I am trying to discover with assistance and guidance, which begins the process of creating metrics or segments.
The support team is above most platforms I use."
- Fullstory review , Bobbi M.

For very large sites, the volume of captured data can feel overwhelming to filter through; building complex segments and metrics takes time, though Fullstory's customer success team is specifically equipped to help teams develop the workflows that make scale manageable.
Mobile and app recording has limitations compared to the web experience, as app heatmaps don't scroll like their web counterparts, and API-defined pages can be a challenge for teams with limited post-implementation resources, though it remains a solid option for web-first teams with mixed mobile needs.

"The app implementation has been a bit difficult. The heatmaps on app only allow you to see the user's screen where it is captured — you can't scroll up and down like you can on the web implementation. Having to use the API to define pages on app can be challenging for teams with limited post-implementation resources."

Using Glassbox feels like having superpowers when it comes to understanding how users interact with our site. It holds a strong 4.9/5 rating on G2 with over 800 reviews, with real-time reporting and segmentation that's useful for tying replays to funnels and spotting drop-offs fast.
Where Glassbox genuinely stands apart is in its capture completeness .
Unlike most tools that sample a percentage of sessions, Glassbox captures 100% of user interactions across web and mobile with no sampling.
Every session is stored, indexed, and instantly retrievable, which matters enormously for financial services, insurance, and healthcare teams that may need to surface a specific session for compliance, fraud investigation, or dispute resolution.
The AI assistant (GIA) adds another layer of utility.
It can quickly summarize sessions or surface common threads across multiple user issues, saving significant time when pattern-finding or making sense of complex journeys.
Interaction maps visualize hotspots and friction without manual tagging, and features like struggle scores and fraud indicators help surface problems and risks that teams didn't even know existed.
The automatic data protection layer is another reason regulated industries trust Glassbox specifically.
PII, PCI, PHI, and NPI masking is built into the platform architecture rather than configured as an add-on, which means sensitive data is protected without teams having to set up and maintain custom redaction rules.
For organizations in financial services, insurance, or healthcare where a missed masking rule can create compliance exposure, that architectural default matters significantly.
Finding specific sessions can take longer than expected, and the experience can feel sluggish when searching by client-specific information or loading detailed replays.
Several G2 reviewers note that some sessions don't always load completely, adding friction when trying to trace an exact user path.
Once past that search and load step, the depth of insight is strong, and the GIA assistant helps surface patterns without requiring teams to manually review every session individually.
G2 review data consistently frames Glassbox as a strong choice for revenue-focused digital experience analytics. With a clear plan for retention needs and a few workflow tweaks, teams get rich behavioral context that accelerates troubleshooting and optimization.
What I like about Glassbox:
I really appreciate that Glassbox captures every single session without sampling. When I need to pull up a specific user's journey for investigation, it's always there.
The GIA assistant saves me from having to watch dozens of replays manually. It flags where users are getting stuck and surfaces patterns across sessions, which means I'm spending time acting on insights rather than hunting for them.

The AI struggle detection is like having a sixth sense for friction points.

No guessing.

Advanced filters and navigation aren't always intuitive for new users, and a step-by-step guided onboarding flow would help non-technical teammates get oriented faster. Once past the initial curve, the platform's depth pays off quickly for teams investigating complex user journeys.

Using Contentsquare feels like finally having that long-overdue conversation with your website where it tells you everything your users are doing, why they're leaving, and where the bottlenecks really are.
Contentsquare is also one of the more affordable session replay services for medium-sized ecommerce sites, balancing deep analytics with cost-conscious pricing models.
What often seals the deal is the data visualization layer.
The platform converts dense behavioral data into accessible charts, heatmaps, and dashboards that are easy to interpret and to present to stakeholders.
The CS Live capability inside the browser provides real-time feedback during launches or major campaigns, saving valuable time when rapid iteration matters most.
A standout development from early 2026 is Contentsquare's MCP integration with Microsoft Copilot.
Teams can now pull behavioral data directly via Copilot without switching platforms, which several G2 reviewers describe as a significant time-saver for reporting.
Where Contentsquare goes further than standard behavioral tools is in its zone-based heatmaps tied to business impact.
Rather than just showing where users click, it quantifies what each zone on a page contributes to conversions and revenue.
Teams can see not just that a section is being ignored, but what it's costing them in missed engagement.
That shift from "here's what users did" to "here's the revenue implication" is what makes Contentsquare particularly well-suited for ecommerce and growth teams prioritizing optimizations by business impact rather than gut feel.
Training proves smooth in practice.
By using CS Academy and recorded sessions, teams can get up to speed faster than expected.
The Customer Success team often goes above and beyond, readily walking through setups and offering proactive tips, and the CS Community serves as a reliable fallback for niche questions or seeing how other organizations tackle similar challenges.
Page mapping and configuration require meaningful effort.
Setting up zoning, segments, and exclusion rules involves real complexity, and teams often find themselves creating segments just to run basic comparisons.
It's less of a daily friction point and more of an upfront setup cost, and with Contentsquare's AI beginning to automate parts of the mapping process, the workload is trending in the right direction for new implementations.
Notable patterns in G2 reviews describe Contentsquare as a strong, enterprise-ready choice for customer journey insight. Once integrations are in place, teams value the depth of analysis and the way findings translate into prioritized, high-impact UX improvements.

I love how the zone-based heatmaps connect directly to business impact. It's not just showing me where users click, it's showing me what those clicks are worth in conversions and revenue, which makes prioritization so much easier.
The CS Live feature inside the browser is genuinely useful during launches. I can see real-time behavioral feedback without leaving my workflow, which saves a lot of time when rapid iteration matters.
